coherence.reasons: Both run diagnosis → rejection of the draft plan → sized levers → first moves → asks, on the same ratio bridge. X's governing thought (firm levers reach ~2.6%, a prepared second wave closes the gap) matches its own arithmetic throughout: $7.7M baseline + $30.1M = $37.8M, with a $5–6M gap. Its flaws are a slide 11 title saying the plan 'reaches 3.0%' when that needs wave 2, and slightly misplaced section labels in the summary. Y's headline ('3% target is reachable', ~3.2% 'at FY2025 scale') sits in tension with its own risk page. There the known 2027 wage step costs ~$6.7M, which puts the base plan at about 2.7% unless the contingency levers also deliver. So Y's top-line claim is not fully carried by its lower-level evidence. Y also sizes levers on $1,503M of sales but computes margin on $1,441M.

judgment.reasons: Both recommend essentially the answer key's preferred plan: promotion pruning, vendor funding, shrink, private label, delivery repricing, six lease-expiry exits, and targeted rather than across-the-board labour. Both keep delivery and defer the three long-lease stores to a board vote. X weighs alternatives more fully. It models the draft plan to FY2028, and it holds a click-and-collect-only option as an explicit fallback that needs the owners' consent. It rejects deeper promotions with a break-even test, and explains why not to exit all nine stores now (payback ~3.4 years, 44% of the one-time budget). X is also candid that firm levers fall short of 3.0% and sets a mid-FY2027 checkpoint with a trigger. Y's judgment is sound but more optimistic: it treats the 2027 wage rise as a risk rather than a baseline item. Its contingency levers (shrink to 2.1%, promo share to 25%) are thinly supported, and it leaves the ValuMart traffic risk unsized. Y does better in one place: it explicitly asks to restore hours in the low-labour stores in the first 90 days.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core numbers right: the bridge (−$15.3M gross margin, −$12.6M e-commerce, −$4.5M labour), the promo/shrink/private-label split, the −$10.4M e-commerce drag, −$12.34 per delivered order, and $6.6M / $4.4M for closures. X uses the evidence more deeply and more carefully. It splits labour into wage (+1.11 pts) and productivity (−0.77 pts) and notes total hours were roughly flat. Y says Harlow 'already cut hours 6%', which conflates hours per $1,000 of sales with total hours. X tests the category team's claim with a break-even calculation and calls it correlation; Y only calls it correlation. X reconciles the 6.1% claim step by step (−$0.5M after delivery, −$10.4M after cannibalisation) and gives break-even incrementality (94% for delivery, 39% for click-and-collect). X sizes levers on the post-exit sales base, nets the cost of reinvested hours against the shrink gain, and gives low/base/high ranges and a sensitivity table. Y's shrink leak (0.5 pts ÷ 6% × 8% = ~$10M) is a crude time-series extrapolation, though flagged as an upper bound. Y's shrink lever has no cost for added hours and assumes $2.3M in FY2026 with little basis. Leaving the known wage step out of the headline flatters Y's 3.2%. X's ~$35M gap differs from the key's ~$30M only because it explicitly adds the wage and delivery-rate headwinds, which is transparent and defensible.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage-inflation hypothesis using a quantified bridge: labour is 13% of the decline, and hours per $1,000 of sales fell. Both reject the 8% cut on shrink grounds, replace the freeze with repricing, and keep a targeted labour element. X goes further. It shows why the dollar view misleads (+$14.3M of labour, only $4.5M of it excess). It projects the draft plan to ~1.1% in FY2028 including the wage step and shrink. It also tests and revises its own margin-first hypothesis, concluding that promotions and delivery alone are not enough. Y's revision is sound but thinner. Its claim that the draft plan 'tops out at ~2%' leaves out the wage step, and its ~$10M shrink leak rests on a looser inference.

overall.reasons: Both documents meet the key's criteria for a defensible conclusion: a quantified bridge, sized levers, the covenant in view, and second-order effects acknowledged. X would serve the CEO better in front of the board and the lender. It is honest that firm levers reach ~2.6% after known headwinds and that a second wave is needed. It gives ranges, sensitivities with triggers, a mid-FY2027 checkpoint and a costed fallback (click-and-collect only), and its rebuttals of the e-commerce and category team claims are more rigorous. Y is tighter and easier to absorb, and its ask to restore hours in lean stores is good. But its headline of 3.2% depends on ignoring the 2027 wage rise in the base case and on less-supported contingency levers, which makes it less credible under scrutiny.
